title: Still venial by nature: endless hell-penalty for it is only accidental
source_text: XXII. Inde tamen sequi negant peccatum veniale natura sua veniale non esse, & ex se poenam aeternam mereri. Quoniam qui non sunt in peccato mortali, si venialiter peccent, non propterea privantur gratia, charitate, & vita spirituali: ac proinde in iis peccatum istud facile tolli & deleri potest, per aliquem dilectionis & contritionis actum. Quo posito, etiamsi Deus poenae isti peccato debitae nihil condonare vellet, non ad poenam aeternam, sed ad poenam tantum temporalem obligati manerent. Quod autem in damnatis peccatum istud, nec quoad culpam tolli, nec etiam quoad poenam remitti potest; id esse tantum per accidens, & quia in illis conjunctum reperitur cum peccatis mortalibus, propter quae sunt in aeternum Dei gratia, & vita spirituali privati.
pass_a_gloss: Yet from that they deny it follows that venial sin is not venial by its own nature, and merits eternal punishment of itself. Because those who are not in mortal sin, if they sin venially, are not for that reason deprived of grace, charity, and spiritual life: and therefore in them that sin can easily be taken away and blotted out by some act of love and contrition. Which being supposed, even if God should will to forgive nothing of the punishment due to that sin, they would remain bound not to eternal punishment, but only to temporal punishment. But that in the damned that sin can neither be taken away as to guilt nor even remitted as to punishment—that is only by accident, and because in them it is found joined with mortal sins, on account of which they are forever deprived of God’s grace and of spiritual life.
pass_b_english: Perpetual hell-penalty for venial sin does not prove it merits hell of itself—the stuckness is accidental to dying in mortal sin.
In the living not under mortal sin, love and contrition can clear venial fault; unpaid debt would still be only temporal.

choices.why: Scholastic contrast with per se desert.
